query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor reactive element addition (e.g., 1–2 at.% yttrium) during synthesis of the refractory high-entropy alloy will form a fine dispersion of Y2O3 nanoparticles, which will improve high‐temperature mechanical capability (through creep and dislocation climb resistance) without appreciably increasing the alloy density or degrading room-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory high-entropy alloy intended for jet-turbine applications with balanced (but not optimized) high-temperature and room-temperature properties.
generation.intervention: Add 1–2 at.% yttrium during alloy melting and subsequent processing to promote in situ formation of finely dispersed Y2O3 particles.
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated under high-temperature conditions (approx. 1000°C) under sustained creep or stress loading and at ambient temperature under standard tensile testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Finely dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles uniformly distributed in the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The in situ formed Y2O3 particles act as obstacles to grain-boundary sliding and dislocation climb at high temperatures, thereby increasing creep resistance, while their limited volume fraction maintains the alloy’s density and room-temperature ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: At high temperatures (around 1000°C), the Y-added alloy should exhibit improved creep resistance—estimated at an improvement on the order of 20-30% relative to the baseline—without a measurable loss in room-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloy produced without the yttrium addition, exhibiting lower high-temperature mechanical stability.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only if the yttrium addition results in a uniform dispersion of nanoscale oxides rather than large agglomerates, and only within the specified concentration range to avoid significant changes in density or deleterious effects on low-temperature ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal yttrium content and the exact improvement magnitude at high temperature remain uncertain due to possible variations in oxide particle size distribution and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set with the addition of 1–2 at.% yttrium and one baseline set without yttrium. Process both sets under identical conditions to ensure similar microstructures aside from the oxide dispersion. Subject the samples to high-temperature creep tests at 1000°C under a controlled constant load, as well as room-temperature tensile tests, and perform microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) to evaluate the dispersion and size of oxide particles.
measurements: Particle size distribution and dispersion uniformity from TEM analyses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-added alloy does not achieve at least a 20% improvement in creep resistance at 1000°C relative to the baseline, or if its room-temperature performance is significantly degraded, or if oxide particles are not uniformly dispersed, then the hypothesis is falsified.
